explain.text:
Figure 2 shows the basic building block of a residual network. The input x enters two weight layers with a ReLU between them, and that stack computes F(x), the residual function. In parallel, a shortcut connection carries x around those layers unchanged, labeled "identity". The two paths meet at an element-wise addition, giving F(x) + x, and a second ReLU is applied after the sum.

The idea behind it, as the paper explains, is that instead of asking the stacked layers to fit a desired mapping H(x) directly, they fit the difference F(x) := H(x) − x, and the original mapping is recovered as F(x) + x p. 2. If an identity mapping were optimal, the layers would only need to push the residual toward zero, which the authors hypothesize is easier than fitting an identity with nonlinear layers p. 2.

In equation form this is y = F(x, {Wi}) + x, with F = W2σ(W1x) for this two-layer case, where σ is ReLU and biases are omitted eq. 1. The shortcut adds no parameters and no computation beyond the addition p. 3.

ask.text:
Right after the circled plus, the summed signal F(x) + x goes through a ReLU, and that output leaves the block. That is the second nonlinearity in the block, applied after the addition rather than before it. The paper states this directly: "We adopt the second nonlinearity after the addition (i.e., σ(y), see Fig. 2)" p. 3.

So the first ReLU sits between the two weight layers inside F, while the second acts on the combined result. Because the ReLU comes after the sum, the shortcut path itself carries x with no transformation until it is added in.

The paper does not explain in this section why the ReLU is placed after the addition rather than elsewhere. It only says this is the choice adopted.

explain.text:
The dotted arrows mark shortcuts where the dimensions increase. In the figure, each one jumps over a block whose first conv has a stride of 2 and doubles the filter count (the "3x3 conv, 128, /2", "256, /2" and "512, /2" boxes). There the input x and the output of the stacked layers no longer have matching shapes, so the plain identity addition of eq. 1 cannot be used. The document offers two fixes: option A keeps the identity and pads extra zero entries, and option B uses the projection W_s of eq. 2, done with 1x1 convolutions. In both, the shortcut goes across feature maps of two sizes with a stride of 2 p. 4. Solid arrows are plain identity shortcuts.

Counting the dotted arrows in the right-hand column, there are three: one into the 128-filter stage, one into the 256-filter stage, and one into the 512-filter stage. The first stage (64 filters) needs none because the pooling layer before it already gives matching dimensions.

This count matches the text's remark that option C, which makes all shortcuts projections, involves thirteen projection shortcuts p. 6. Those thirteen would be the three dotted ones plus the ten solid ones in the right column, giving sixteen in total, so the figure and text are consistent with 16 shortcuts overall.

ask.text:
The dotted arrows are shortcuts where the dimensions increase. Each one skips a pair of 3x3 layers whose first conv is the "/2" box (128, 256 and 512 filters). The input and output shapes then differ, so plain identity addition can't be used. The document offers two fixes: zero-padding the extra entries (option A) or a 1x1 projection (option B), both applied with a stride of 2 p. 4. Solid arrows are ordinary identity shortcuts.

Counting the right-hand column, there are 3 dotted arrows, one into each of the 128, 256 and 512 stages. There are also 13 solid ones (3 in the 64 stage, 3 in the 128 stage, 5 in the 256 stage, 2 in the 512 stage), so 16 shortcuts in total.

That corrects my earlier remark. The thirteen projection shortcuts mentioned for option C p. 6 match the 13 solid arrows, not "3 dotted plus 10 solid". The document doesn't say why it counts thirteen when option C makes all shortcuts projections. From general knowledge, the likely reading is that thirteen refers to the extra projections C adds beyond B's three dotted ones.

explain.text:
Figure 4 plots error (%) against training iterations (in units of 10^4) on ImageNet. Thin curves are training error and bold curves are validation error on center crops p. 5. The left panel shows plain 18- and 34-layer nets; the right shows ResNets of the same depths.

On the left, the 34-layer plain net (red) sits above the 18-layer one (cyan) for most of training. Its thin training curve is higher throughout, and its bold validation curve ends around 32 to 33% against roughly 31% for the 18-layer net. That is the degradation problem: the deeper net is worse even on training error, so overfitting is not the cause p. 5.

On the right, the order flips. ResNet-34 is below ResNet-18, with validation error ending near 28% versus about 31%, and its training error is lower still, around 25%. So the added depth now helps, which the text says shows degradation is addressed here p. 5.

The sharp drops near 15 and 30 (x10^4) are the learning rate being divided by 10 when error plateaus p. 4. The 18-layer ResNet also falls faster early on than plain-18 p. 6.

Table 2 reports the final numbers: 27.94 and 28.54 for plain-18 and plain-34, and 27.88 and 25.03 for ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 p. 5. These are 10-crop errors, so they differ from the center-crop curves plotted here.

ask.text:
In both panels the error falls off a cliff at about 15 and again at about 30 on the x-axis, which is roughly 150,000 and 300,000 iterations since the axis is in units of 1e4. The first drop is the larger one, taking the bold curves from the low 50s (plain) or mid 40s (ResNet) down to around 35 to 40%. The second is smaller, bringing them to roughly 31 to 33%.

The cause is the learning-rate schedule. The paper says the learning rate starts at 0.1 and is divided by 10 when the error plateaus p. 4. Each drop marks one of those divisions. At the high rate the error stalls, and cutting the rate lets the solver settle into a lower region.

The document does not say the exact iteration numbers of the changes, only that they occur at plateaus, so reading them as about 15 and 30 comes from the figure itself. The same steps appear in all four curves, which fits a schedule shared by all the networks rather than something specific to depth.

explain.text:
Figure 6 shows CIFAR-10 training curves, with iterations (in units of 1e4) on the x-axis and error (%) on the y-axis. Dashed lines are training error and bold lines are test error p. 8.

Left panel, plain nets of 20, 32, 44 and 56 layers: going deeper makes things worse. The 56-layer net ends at roughly 13% test error, while the 20-layer net sits near 10%. The training curves show the same ordering, with plain-56 training error well above plain-20's. This is the degradation problem, since the deeper net is worse even on the training set, so it is not simple overfitting. The caption adds that plain-110 was above 60% and is left out.

Middle panel, ResNets of the same depths plus 110: the ordering flips. Deeper nets reach lower error, with ResNet-110 lowest at about 6.5% test error and ResNet-20 highest at about 9%. All the training curves fall close to zero. The sharp drops near iteration 3.2e4 are the learning-rate decreases (divide by 10 at 32k and 48k iterations) p. 7.

Right panel, ResNet-110 against ResNet-1202: both reach very low training error (the 1202-layer net below 0.1%), but the 1202-layer net has higher test error, about 8% against 6.5%. The document attributes this to overfitting from an unnecessarily large model (19.4M parameters) for this small dataset p. 8.

ask.text: The 1202-layer curve is magenta (pink), labelled residual-1202 in the legend. Its bold test-error line sits a little above the 5 gridline and below the 10 gridline, starting around 8.5% and settling near 7.5 to 8% by the end of training. That matches the 7.93% the document reports for this network p. 7. The black residual-110 curve sits lower, around 6.5%, which is the gap the document attributes to overfitting in the larger model p. 8. The magenta dashed training curve is down near zero at the bottom of the panel.

explain.text:
Figure 7 measures how strongly each 3×3 layer responds, using the standard deviation of its output after batch normalization and before ReLU or the addition. For ResNets this is effectively the strength of the residual function F(x) p. 8.

The top panel plots std against layer index in network order. Plain-20 and plain-56 (dashed) mostly sit between about 1.5 and 2.5, with plain-56 reaching roughly 2.2 around layers 20 to 25. The ResNets (solid) mostly hover near 1, with a spike around layer 37 in ResNet-56 and ResNet-110. All curves start high at the first layer, around 3.

The bottom panel sorts each network's layers from largest to smallest response, which makes the comparison cleaner. The plain curves lie above their ResNet counterparts, and ResNet-110 is flattest and lowest, trailing off below 1.

The document's reading is that ResNets have generally smaller responses, supporting the idea that residual functions are closer to zero, and that deeper ResNets (20, 56, 110) modify the signal less per layer p. 8. The document doesn't explain why the first layer is so large.

ask.text:
In the bottom plot, ResNet-110 (the black curve) has the smallest responses overall. After its first few layers it settles just below 1 and drifts down to roughly 0.8 across most of its 110 layers, ending near 0.65. Its tail is the flattest and lowest of the five curves.

ResNet-56 (solid red) is close behind and actually dips lower at the very end, to about 0.65 around layer 55, but across the bulk of its layers it sits slightly above ResNet-110. The plain networks are clearly larger: plain-56 stays around 1 to 2.3 and plain-20 around 1.3 to 2.5.

This matches the document's reading that deeper ResNets, comparing ResNet-20, 56 and 110, have smaller response magnitudes, so each individual layer modifies the signal less p. 8. The figure is only a measurement of response size. The document doesn't say it proves anything beyond supporting that motivation.
